edges.justification: The book‑to‑market ratio reflects firm valuation; high book‑to‑market (value) firms tend to generate higher future returns.
Earnings surprises influence investor expectations and price movements, directly affecting the stock’s annual return.
The month when the fiscal year ends determines the timing of earnings reporting and subsequent price evolution that drives the 12‑month return.
Superior annual performance attracts institutional investors, prompting changes in ownership stakes.
Higher leverage amplifies both risk and potential return, making debt levels a determinant of the stock’s annual return.
The overall market performance exerts a strong influence on individual stock returns.
Momentum effects: prior five‑year performance predicts subsequent one‑year returns.
The quality score incorporates the annual return as a key component of profitability and performance.
Membership in a value index is associated with distinct return dynamics, influencing the stock’s annual performance.
Value firms often experience larger earnings surprises because analysts’ expectations differ from those of growth firms.
The fiscal year end month dictates the timing of book value reporting, thereby affecting the book‑to‑market ratio.
A high book‑to‑market ratio signals investment attractiveness, which can drive institutional ownership changes.
Firms with higher book‑to‑market ratios tend to maintain lower debt levels to preserve equity quality.
Book‑to‑market is a core component of the quality score’s valuation dimension.
Value index membership is defined by the book‑to‑market ratio.
Timing of the fiscal year end affects debt reporting and therefore the calculated leverage ratio.
The fiscal year end determines when the quality score is computed.
Updates to index membership are made in alignment with the fiscal year end.
Institutional ownership changes are measured over the 12 months following the fiscal year end.
Historical performance informs valuation expectations, influencing the book‑to‑market ratio.
Past returns shape capital structure decisions, affecting the leverage ratio.
Historical performance may affect a firm’s inclusion in a value index.
Past returns correlate with profitability metrics that feed into the quality score.
Prior returns attract institutional investors, prompting ownership changes.
A firm’s debt level influences earnings expectations and can affect the magnitude of earnings surprises.
Low leverage is a criterion in the quality score calculation.
Index membership tends to attract institutional portfolio managers, leading to ownership changes.
Surprise earnings events trigger institutional trading decisions.
Earnings surprises influence the profitability component of the quality score.
Overall market performance guides institutional portfolio rebalancing.
Higher quality scores attract institutional investors, causing ownership changes.
The market return component of beta is part of the quality score calculation.
